Commitment "%(n)s" is measured as a percentage, so the level has to lie between 0 and 100; it is %(m)s.
Per the "Priority scope for development and demo" section of the catalogue document. 0 means unranked.
Period %(k)s runs on cycle "%(c)s" but the contract has no commitment assessed on that cycle.
Leave it empty and the commitment applies to EVERY plant in the contract scope, with a result row of its own for each.
Some rows could not be measured, or the unattributed hours exceed the threshold. The figures for this period are not yet fit to sign.
The unattributed hours exceed this commitment's threshold. The availability figure may be flattering simply because nobody has classified them.
Rounded to the number of decimal places the contract declares. This is the figure that goes into the certificate AND the figure used to compute the penalty.
Period %s is closed. The figures have been captured as a certificate and cannot be measured again — reopen the period first if it really is necessary.
Periods run from the EFFECTIVE DATE, not the calendar year. A contract signed on 15 April has a contract year running 15 April → 14 April.
What a contract of this type has to be able to track. Used as a checklist during a survey, not as contract terms.
Whether the system can measure this basis at all. If it cannot, the period still produces a result row stating the reason, and NO penalty is charged.
Closing the period freezes the committed levels, the measured figures and the fee for this period. Editing the contract afterwards no longer changes this period's certificate.
Per point: an amount for each percentage point of shortfall. As a %% of the period fee: a percentage of the fee per point of shortfall. Fixed: an amount.
When the unattributed hours exceed this share of total downtime, the result row raises a flag. The result is still computed, but whoever signs the certificate sees it before signing.
The fee used as the base for capping the penalty. For a fee-bearing period it is the plant's period fee; for an assessment-only period it is the total fee of the fee periods it covers.
Turn it off when the contract type already has a home of its own. The type stays in the catalogue so the whole picture is visible, but it cannot be chosen when raising an O&M contract.
Type "%s" is marked as not managed here, so it has to say where it is managed. Leave it empty and a user meets a type they cannot choose, with no idea where to go instead.
Only a period on the contract's own cycle carries a fee. A period on another cycle is for assessment only — charging for both is charging twice for the same stretch of time.
Availability and performance are "at least"; response and repair time are "must not exceed". Choose the wrong direction and every period that passed now fails, and the other way round.
Capped against the plant's period fee. 0 means NO cap — use it only when the contract genuinely has none, because without a cap one bad period produces a penalty larger than the fee itself.
Commitment "%s" declares a penalty regime but the rate is 0 — every period that fails produces a penalty of 0 with nothing to say so. Set "No penalty" if the contract has no regime.
The operating phase has many kinds of contract, not just one overall O&M agreement. Any type that already has a home of its own (power purchase, EPC, lending) cannot be chosen here.
Commitment "%(n)s" points at plant "%(p)s", which is not within the contract scope. Add that plant to the scope first, otherwise the commitment will never produce a result row.

Contract "%(h)s" declares an invalid time zone "%(t)s". Measuring a period in the wrong time zone shifts downtime into the neighbouring period, so it stops here rather than producing a figure that looks ordinary.
This screen answers exactly the question the customer asks: what does this\n plant owe for this period — fee less penalty, per plant, even when one\n contract covers several plants.

Declare the plant scope, the commitments and the penalty regime once. Every period after that is one press of Measure the period: the system takes the figures from the outage log, compares them with the commitments and produces the amount payable for each plant.

The number of units used as the DENOMINATOR when computing time-based availability. Thirty turbines running for one day is 720 unit-hours, not 24. 0 means the whole plant counts as ONE unit — which is right only when the commitment is set at plant level.

Type "%(l)s" is not managed here — it lives in: %(d)s. It stays in the catalogue so the whole picture is visible, but the contract has to be raised in the right place; otherwise the same contract exists in two copies and neither is the real one.

The operating phase has many kinds of contract, not just one overall O&M agreement. A greyed-out row is a type that already has a home of its own — kept in the catalogue so the whole picture is visible, but raise the contract where it belongs.

The O&M fee for this plant alone in one period. Declared per plant rather than as one lump: a contract covering three plants with only a single total cannot answer the question "what does this plant owe this month" — and that is exactly the question the customer asks.

Leave it empty to follow the contract's own cycle. Set it when the contract has SEVERAL tiers of commitment — wind usually has both a monthly floor and an annual availability. Assessing an annual commitment with one month's figures penalises unfairly: one bad month drags the whole year down, while the contract allows the remaining months to make up for it.

OFF by default: only downtime hours attributed to an O&M contract obligation count against the contractor. Turn it on when the contract makes the contractor liable by default until proven otherwise. On or off, the unattributed hours still appear on the result row — an availability figure that is flattering because nobody has classified them has to be visible.

This is a contract table of O&M's own, not shared with EPC contracts. An EPC contract is a one-way journey with gates; an O&M contract is a repeating service, and what decides the money is the figure measured in the period.

This period has rows that could not be measured, or a great many downtime hours with no responsibility attributed. The availability figure may be flattering because nobody has classified them rather than because the contractor did well — look at the "Unattributed (%)" column before taking this certificate to be signed.

This type already has a home of its own, so it cannot be chosen when raising an O&M contract. It stays in the catalogue so the whole contract picture of the operating phase is visible — raise it in two places and the same contract has two copies, neither of them the real one.

A greyed-out row is a commitment the system could not measure. The period still produces a result row for it, states the reason and charges no penalty — rather than quietly substituting another basis. Two bases give two different figures, and taking the wrong one charges the wrong money while the certificate still looks complete.

A period is written in DATES while the outage log is written in UTC moments, so midnight of the period has to be midnight somewhere definite. Declared on the contract itself rather than taken from whoever is logged in: if the same period measured by two people in two time zones gives two figures, no certificate stands up. A user who has declared no time zone makes Odoo treat everything as UTC — seven hours out, and those seven hours shift downtime into the neighbouring period exactly at the contract-year boundary.

The measured figure is ROUNDED to here before being compared with the commitment and before the penalty is computed. The reason: if the certificate prints 97.66 against a commitment of 99.5, the contractor will work out the penalty by hand — and if the system used 97.664765 instead, the two numbers disagree and nobody can defend the certificate. The number on the paper has to be the number used in the arithmetic. Changing this field can turn a borderline period from pass to fail, so it belongs to the contract rather than being a display option.

Availability units is the denominator, and this is the quietest place to get it wrong: thirty turbines running for one day is 720 unit-hours, not 24. 0 means the whole plant counts as one unit — right only when the contract commits at plant level. The calculator button only counts child locations; not every location is a unit, so the person declaring it still has to decide.
